name: Alumnus A (fictional)
story: Took CS3244 and CS4243 in Year 2, started as an RA in an NLP lab in Year 2 Semester 2, co-authored one workshop paper by Year 3, and is now a PhD student at a fictional overseas university.
advice: Start the RA conversation a full semester before you think you're ready — labs plan their intake in advance.

name: Alumnus B (fictional)
story: Did two ML-adjacent internships (data science, then applied ML), built three portfolio projects on GitHub, and joined a mid-size AI company as an ML engineer straight after graduating.
current_role: ML Engineer at a fictional AI company
advice: One deep project beats three shallow ones on a resume — interviewers ask follow-up questions and shallow projects fall apart fast.

name: Alumnus C (fictional)
story: Joined the Student Founder Track in Year 2, co-founded a small productivity-tools startup with a coursemate, and after graduating raised a small pre-seed round from a fictional local fund.
advice: Ship something small and real before you write a business plan. The plan changes; the muscle of shipping doesn't.

name: Alumnus D (fictional)
story: Switched from an industry-track internship search to an RA position after realizing they preferred the open-ended problems in the lab; ended up applying to grad school a year later than planned.
advice: It's fine to change paths mid-degree — the switch cost you one internship cycle, not the whole degree.

name: Alumnus E (fictional)
story: Prioritized systems/infra modules over pure ML theory, interned on a platform team, and is now working on ML infrastructure rather than model-building directly.
advice: 'AI industry' isn't just modeling roles — infra and tooling roles are less competitive and just as central to shipping AI products.

name: Alumnus F (fictional)
story: Entered three case competitions and one hackathon in Year 1-2 before finding a co-founder at a pitch night; the eventual startup idea had nothing to do with any of those competitions.
advice: Competitions are for meeting people and building reps, not for finding your idea directly — don't be discouraged if the idea doesn't come from one.

name: Alumnus G (fictional)
story: Kept CAP above 4.5 while doing a light RA load (5 hrs/week) for three semesters, which kept the option open for both grad school and a research-heavy industry role.
advice: You don't have to choose between CAP and research early on — a light, sustained RA commitment is easier to keep up than people assume.

name: Alumnus H (fictional)
story: Took a CCA leadership role that had nothing to do with AI, and found it came up in every interview as the answer to 'tell me about a time you led something.'
advice: Not every high-leverage move has to be technical — a leadership story is a gap most AI-focused students have.
